source.title: Archetypal SAE: Adaptive and Stable Dictionary Learning for Concept Extraction in Large Vision Models
source.authors: Thomas Fel; E. Lubana; Jacob S. Prince; Matthew Kowal; Victor Boutin; Isabel Papadimitriou; Binxu Wang; Martin Wattenberg; Demba E. Ba; Talia Konkle

record.file_problem: No apparent garbling or wrong-document issue. The supplied text includes the paper and appendices; the final table is cut off, but the results relevant to the recorded rows are present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper directly measures dictionary stability across training runs and tests recovery of known concepts with SAE dictionaries. Its results qualify claims that SAE features are stable, canonical units, while proposing a method that improves stability.
record.gate_note: The paper does not test toy-model superposition, feature overlap as a function of sparsity or importance, or feature dimensionality. The results in Table 2 are omitted because the flattened layout does not support reliable assignment of its values to conditions. Cited results from other work are not recorded.
record.test_reason: The study measures run-to-run stability of standard SAE dictionaries on vision models and tests whether SAEs recover known concepts. Standard SAEs reach stability of about 0.54–0.71 and barely beat PCA or K-Means on concept recovery. This directly qualifies V5's claim that dictionary features are stable, canonical units. Most other rows report the authors' own A-SAE/RA-SAE method.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is essentially correct. The authors frame instability as a fundamental limitation: identical training runs can yield divergent SAE dictionaries. They report that archetypal constraints (A-SAE/RA-SAE) restore stability while matching reconstruction, and improve plausibility and identifiability scores in large vision models.
record.recipe_differences: The study learns SAE dictionaries for vision-model activations and constrains decoder atoms to convex combinations of data points, with an optional relaxation. It does not reproduce the original toy-network superposition method.
record.method_sensitivity: Dictionary stability varies by SAE method. The paper also evaluates archetypal variants with different relaxation strengths, but the relevant Table 2 values are not assigned to conditions because the supplied table layout is ambiguous.
record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 267, 2025
record.problems: The reported stability and benchmark scores have no uncertainty estimates in the supplied text. The concept-recovery benchmark uses synthetic collages and does not establish that recovered concepts are complete or canonical units of natural model representations. The supplied Table 2 layout is ambiguous.
record.rows_left_out: Table 2 plausibility results were not recorded because the flattened layout does not reliably assign the values to models and relaxation settings. No other relevant result rows were omitted.

untested.parts: All of it: no toy models, sparsity transition or feature geometry.
All of it: capacity competition and feature importance are not studied.
All of it: neuron polysemanticity is not studied.
Only vision models are studied; there are no LLM results.
Completeness of SAE dictionaries and canonicity across dictionary sizes; all results are on vision models, none on LLMs.
All of it: feature dimensionality is not studied.

missing.what: Plausibility benchmark. TopK SAE alignment with classifier-head directions stays low and flat as the dictionary grows: about 0.17 on ConvNeXt from 512 to 32k atoms, versus about 0.40 for A-SAE. The authors note limited alignment for classical SAEs even with very large dictionaries. This bears on V5's completeness and canonicity; the verdict here is based on the text.
Stability across 4–5 models and 5 sparsity levels for all methods, plus the data-perturbation (5–10%) result showing a similar instability trend.
Max Cosine (best single match) stays at 0.993–0.997 for standard SAEs even though global stability is low, so some concepts do recur across runs.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'supports' label was replaced. The A-SAE/RA-SAE rows are the authors' own method, stable by construction, so they show stability depends on a design choice rather than that SAE features are canonical units. Table 2 is in fact readable for the TopK baseline rows and should be extracted. The rows contain no uncertainty estimates.

versions.untested_parts: Whether sparse features exceeding network dimensions are stored as overlapping, nearly orthogonal directions; sparsity-dependent transitions and regular geometry.
Whether polysemanticity arises from capacity competition or whether feature importance determines dedicated versus shared dimensions.
Whether polysemantic neurons arise through mechanisms other than capacity pressure.
The claim is specifically about LLMs; this study evaluates vision models, not LLMs.

The study measures run-to-run dictionary stability and recovery of known concepts in synthetic image benchmarks. It does not establish that SAE features are globally complete or canonical units of a model's representation.
Whether the represented features are one-dimensional directions rather than multidimensional features.

relation.reason: The study measures standard-SAE dictionary stability and recovery of known generative concepts.

tranche.reason: Standard-SAE seed instability and incomplete known-concept recovery directly qualify V5.

source_check.notes: Stability is optimal matched mean cosine, not a fraction of identical concepts; identifiability is threshold-optimized class accuracy with dictionary size equal to the known object count. Tables 1 and 3 provide comparisons without a designated baseline; reconstruction parity is specifically established for relaxed RA-SAE.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Standard SAE methods on DINOv2, across training runs
reader_labels.reason: The paper reports low stability for standard SAEs, with scores 0.710, 0.542, and 0.539, and describes substantial differences between rerun dictionaries (r1-r3).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: RA-SAE stability on DINOv2 and object recovery in the tested synthetic image benchmarks
reader_labels.reason: RA-SAE has a stability score of 0.927, and archetypal variants achieve high object-concept identification accuracy across four vision models (r4, r7, r10, r13, r16).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Soft Identifiability benchmark, compared with TopK SAE
reader_labels.reason: TopK scores are lower than archetypal variants, and the benchmark only tests recovery of known object classes in synthetic image mixtures; it does not establish complete or canonical model-wide units (r5, r8, r11, r14).
